concepts.name: Neural Machine Translation (NMT)
concepts.definition: A machine translation approach that uses a single neural network to directly model the probability of translating a source sentence into a target sentence, replacing traditional rule-based or statistical methods.
concepts.intuition: Think of NMT as a bilingual student who learns to translate by reading thousands of paired sentences, gradually improving without needing explicit grammar rules.
concepts.importance: It simplifies translation systems by unifying components into one end-to-end model, enabling better learning of complex language patterns.
concepts.example: Translating 'I love cats' from English to French as 'J'aime les chats' using one neural network.

concepts.name: Encoder-Decoder Architecture
concepts.definition: A neural network structure consisting of an encoder that compresses input data into a context vector and a decoder that generates output from that vector.
concepts.intuition: Like summarizing a book into one sentence (encoder) and then rewriting the whole story from that summary (decoder).
concepts.importance: It forms the foundational framework for sequence-to-sequence tasks like translation, summarization, and speech recognition.
concepts.example: An RNN reads 'The cat is sleeping' and outputs a vector; another RNN uses that vector to generate 'Le chat dort'.

concepts.name: Fixed-Length Vector
concepts.definition: A single, static-size vector representation of an entire input sequence, used as the sole communication channel between encoder and decoder.
concepts.intuition: Trying to fit an entire library into a single sticky note — you lose details as the book gets longer.
concepts.importance: It creates a bottleneck for long sentences, limiting translation quality because too much information is compressed into one vector.
concepts.example: Encoding 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' into a 512-dimensional vector, losing nuances of word order or emphasis.

concepts.name: Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)
concepts.definition: A type of neural network designed to process sequential data by maintaining a hidden state that captures information from previous time steps.
concepts.intuition: Like reading a sentence word by word, remembering each word to understand the next — your brain keeps a running summary.
concepts.importance: RNNs enabled early NMT models to handle variable-length inputs, but suffer from vanishing gradients and poor long-range dependency capture.
concepts.example: An RNN reads 'I went to the store' one word at a time, updating its hidden state after each word.

concepts.name: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
concepts.definition: An advanced RNN variant with memory cells and gates that selectively retain or forget information over long sequences.
concepts.intuition: Like a smart notetaker who remembers important details and ignores distractions during a long lecture.
concepts.importance: LSTMs improved RNN performance on translation by mitigating vanishing gradients, enabling better modeling of long sentences.
concepts.example: An LSTM remembers 'cat' from the start of a sentence to correctly translate 'The cat that I saw yesterday is sleeping'.

concepts.name: Sequence-to-Sequence Learning
concepts.definition: A machine learning paradigm where an input sequence (e.g., source sentence) is mapped to an output sequence (e.g., translation).
concepts.intuition: Like converting a melody played on piano into sheet music — same information, different format.
concepts.importance: It provides the general framework for tasks like translation, summarization, and chatbots, where input and output are both sequences.

concepts.name: Conditional Probability in Translation
concepts.definition: The probability of a target sentence y given a source sentence x, formalized as p(y|x), which NMT models aim to maximize.
concepts.intuition: What’s the most likely way to say this in French, given that I said 'I need coffee' in English?
concepts.importance: It defines the objective of translation: not just matching words, but choosing the most probable and natural output.
concepts.example: For 'She runs fast', p('Elle court vite') > p('Elle va rapidement') — the model picks the more natural translation.

concepts.name: Joint Training
concepts.definition: Training all components of a model (e.g., encoder and decoder) together to optimize a single objective function, rather than separately.
concepts.intuition: Teaching a translator and their assistant to work as a team — they learn from each other’s mistakes in real time.
concepts.importance: Allows the model to adapt encoder representations to decoder needs, improving overall translation quality.
concepts.example: The encoder learns to highlight 'cat' in 'The cat is sleeping' because the decoder needs that word to generate 'le chat'.

concepts.name: Alignment in Translation
concepts.definition: The correspondence between words or phrases in the source sentence and their translations in the target sentence.
concepts.intuition: Like drawing dotted lines between words in English and their French equivalents when learning a new language.
concepts.importance: Explicit alignment helps models know which part of the source to focus on when generating each target word.
concepts.example: In 'I love cats', alignment links 'I'→'Je', 'love'→'aime', 'cats'→'les chats'.

concepts.name: Soft Alignment
concepts.definition: A differentiable, weighted combination of source elements used to inform each target word prediction, without hard segmentation.
concepts.intuition: Instead of pointing at one word, you give attention scores like 70% to 'cat', 20% to 'sleeping', and 10% to 'the' — a smooth blend.
concepts.importance: Enables the model to focus flexibly on relevant parts of long sentences without rigid boundaries, improving accuracy and generalization.
concepts.example: When translating 'The cat that I saw yesterday is sleeping', the model assigns higher weights to 'cat' and 'sleeping' for the target word 'dort'.

concepts.name: Attention Mechanism
concepts.definition: A method that allows a decoder to dynamically weigh and select relevant parts of the encoder’s hidden states when generating each output word.
concepts.intuition: Like a spotlight that moves across the source sentence as you translate — focusing on different words at each step.
concepts.importance: It overcomes the fixed-length vector bottleneck, enabling translation of long sentences and improving performance significantly.
concepts.example: While translating 'The cat is sleeping on the mat', attention focuses on 'sleeping' when generating 'dort', then shifts to 'mat' for 'tapis'.

concepts.name: Context Vector (in Attention)
concepts.definition: A weighted sum of encoder hidden states, computed using attention weights, used as input to the decoder for predicting each target word.
concepts.intuition: Each time you write a new word in translation, you peek at the source sentence and pick only what’s relevant right now — that’s your context.
concepts.importance: It replaces the single fixed vector with a dynamic, word-specific summary of the source, enabling long-range dependencies.
concepts.example: For target word 'dort', context vector = 0.8×h_cat + 0.15×h_sleeping + 0.05×h_the — weighted by attention scores.

concepts.name: Bottleneck in Encoder-Decoder Models
concepts.definition: The limitation caused by forcing all information from a source sentence into a single fixed-length vector, degrading performance on long inputs.
concepts.intuition: Trying to fit a whole movie into one screenshot — you lose plot details, especially if the movie is long.
concepts.importance: This bottleneck motivated the invention of attention, which removed this constraint and revolutionized sequence modeling.
concepts.example: An encoder-decoder model performs poorly on sentences longer than 30 words because critical information gets lost in compression.

concepts.name: Joint Learning to Align and Translate
concepts.definition: A training paradigm where alignment (which source words relate to which target words) and translation are learned simultaneously in one model.
concepts.intuition: Learning to translate by naturally noticing which words go together — like learning a language by immersion, not memorizing rules.
concepts.importance: It eliminates the need for separate alignment tools and enables end-to-end optimization, leading to more accurate and fluent translations.
concepts.example: The model learns that 'quickly' in English often maps to 'rapidement' in French without being told — it discovers the pattern automatically.

concepts.name: Soft Alignment Visualization
concepts.definition: The graphical representation of attention weights showing which source words influenced each generated target word.
concepts.intuition: A heatmap where bright spots show which source words the model 'looked at' when translating each target word.
concepts.importance: It provides interpretability, proving the model learns linguistically meaningful alignments without explicit supervision.
concepts.example: A heatmap shows high attention on 'cat' when generating 'chat', and on 'sleeping' when generating 'dort' — visually validating the translation logic.
